text:
Chapter Thirteen


Maggie busied herself with her coffee, hoping the cool liquid would help the blush creeping up her neck. When it didn’t work, she avoided Taliesin’s confident smirk by looking at the spread-out documents, lab results, and ancient books open on the table.


He had even brought a test tube filled with a viscous liquid that could only be pall slime. She picked it up, running her thumb over the rune keeping the pall contained within the glass, and turned it over to watch the shimmering lavender liquid move from end to end. It was almost pretty when it wasn’t trying to kill you.


“Is your arm bothering you?” Taliesin asked, and she looked down to where she was absentmindedly rubbing where the ghoul had gripped her with its long, knobby fingers.


He had asked after her arm every morning that week. She pushed up her sleeve and showed him what remained. It had faded significantly, with just a hint of red lingering. Her skin was itchy and tight as it healed, but it was more of an annoyance than any true discomfort. “No. It’s much better,” she said. After a moment, she added quietly, “Thank you for asking.”


As she tugged her sleeve back down, he gestured to the documents on the table. “As promised, this is everything I know about the pall so far.” He handed her a stack of file folders. “It will be helpful to have another set of eyes on the data.”


She opened the first folder. The document on top was a summary of the chemical makeup of the pall. She wasn’t surprised to see that it was strangely potent, composed of an unusually high amount of ectoplasm. Taliesin had at least had the sense to set up monitoring equipment, which showed regular off-the-charts electromagnetic readings and dangerously high levels of the unseen elements. Barometric pressure for a full square mile was off-kilter, with readings that explained the low-hanging clouds and drizzling rain that had plagued Galloway in the days after the pall fell.


“How far out are the effects being felt?”


He pointed to a weather radar chart showing a small circle over Galloway. “It’s a small section of town. Essentially the one square mile around Ilex Hall, which includes a small section of downtown Galloway. I consulted with one of the botanists, Dr. Silva, and she assured me that there aren’t widespread ecological implications, especially if we employ mitigation efforts if this drags on through summer to protect plant growth on campus and in Galloway itself. It was one of my first concerns.”


Before she could even ask, Taliesin shuffled the papers again and produced various reports about fantasmia sightings. Maps showing increased activity, data charts, eyewitness accounts, all carefully sorted. The man was organized, and, for some reason, that made her skin flush hot.


“Unfortunately, we are seeing elevated fantasmia activity for about fifteen square miles around Ilex Hall. It’s most prominent in the towns along the edge of the Wilds.” He pointed to a stat showing the incidence of ghoul and banshee sightings. As expected, they were being driven from their nests in the forest, attracted to the pull of the pall. He went on. “Wraith sightings have increased, too, but I am less worried about them. Since your run-in with the ghoul, wardsmiths have been called in from Atlantia and Delphi to strengthen wards on public buildings and private residences within these perimeters.” Maggie narrowed her eyes, but Taliesin answered her question before she could say it out loud. “For free.” He cleared his throat. “We should have done it sooner, but I had hoped to have the situation under control before now.”


Maggie put down the papers she was holding and fanned out another stack. “Can I see the dissipation spells you’ve tried so far?”


He flipped through documents until he found what she was looking for. Unsurprisingly, his equations were elegant. They were detailed and complex, inclusive of all the variables she had thought of and a few she hadn’t. Though she would like someone else to confirm the calculations were correct, she suspected there wouldn’t be a mistake among them.


He reached across the table and pointed to two of the runes. “These I tried with a decoction of gold dust,” he explained. “I found a few promising studies about gold as a conduit for the unseen elements, but it didn’t make a difference.”


Maggie looked at the papers thoughtfully. “And your incantations?”


“I modified the standard dissipation spell to account for the size and severity of the pall, but I’m sure you’d be able to make them even better.”


Sure enough, as she looked over his variations of the dissipation incantation, she could see several places where she would make small, subtle changes. Little translation differences that, in the grand scheme of things, probably wouldn’t change the outcome of the spell.


Even with its size and severity, dissipating this pall should have been simple. Dissipation spells, like banishments, were legacy incantations that had been around as long as there had been magic. Taliesin’s calculations were impeccable. His runes expertly drawn. It didn’t make sense.


Finally, she couldn’t avoid it anymore. She had to know. “Dr. Taliesin,” she began, and he frowned slightly, but she went on. “I need to know. What spell caused this? Class three spells are banned on Hawthorn’s campus without extensive precautions. Why did you do it?”


He sighed, but he had to have known this question was coming. It simply wasn’t possible for her to work on finding a solution to this problem without knowing what caused it in the first place. She tried to soften the harshness in her voice, but her words still had a hard edge to them. “The kind of magic necessary to create a fissure this large…”—she referred back to his own measurements of the crack between this world and the next—“seven feet.” She couldn’t imagine it.


Anyone who studied spellmaking, whether they specialized in incantation translations or runology or alchemy itself, took an entire semester on pall science and dissipation. The largest fissure Maggie had ever seen was around five inches, and this was seven feet. It was unthinkable. A fissure that large between this world and the next…the next world, where souls should be resting.


Maggie swallowed, suddenly feeling sick. “Have you seen unsettled souls in Ilex Hall?” When a pall descended, souls that had moved on to their final resting place could be stirred, slipping through the fissure back into this world. Maggie had never seen an unsettled soul, not even when she had done her required coursework in pall science. But a pall of this strength, a fissure of this size…of course the hall had to be rife with the dead.


There was a pained expression on Taliesin’s face as he nodded. “Every time I’ve been, there are more unsettled,” he admitted, and Maggie could have sworn he was changing the subject when he sighed and went on. “I know I need to tell you what happened.”


“You don’t need to be embarrassed.”


He considered her for a moment. “I’m not embarrassed. That’s not why I haven’t told you—or anyone except Dean Clearwater—what happened.”


“Dean Clearwater knows?”


“Of course. I told him the moment I left the infirmary that day.” He fiddled with his coffee cup, the drink long gone. “About three years ago, at Dartwood, a new spell I was working on for my research went awry and I conjured a pall by mistake. I confined it to a cabinet in my lab so I could use it in a lesson with my undergrads.”


Maggie raised an eyebrow. “So, this is a habit of yours?”


He glanced up at her, and she waited to see his eyes flash with annoyance or even anger, but he just gave her a sad smile and went on. “I carefully warded the lab, set the pall loose, and gave my students fifteen minutes and fifteen minutes only to observe it. They wore masks, gloves, and rune charms to stop the effects of the pall from taking root. We timed their exposure to the second. I had a school counselor on standby, just in case any of the students found the melancholia too upsetting.


“They spent ten minutes taking notes and studying the pall, and in the last five, I demonstrated the dissipation spell. The pall fizzled out quickly, leaving only a bit of slime and a thick coating of dust behind.”


“Why are you telling me this?”


“Because I’m a careful man, Maggie.”


He sighed again, looking off to the side. She was surprised by the pain she saw in the way he narrowed his eyes. It almost looked like grief. When he went on, he still avoided her gaze, staring down at his hands as he laced and unlaced his fingers. “My first mistake was doing the spell at all. But it’s one I have done hundreds of times. One that, I thought, I could do in my sleep.” He paused again. “Are you familiar with my research?”


She laughed a little at that. “Of course I am. Who isn’t?”


“You’d be surprised. I don’t like to assume people care about what I’m doing. That’s a fast way to look like an asshole.”


At that, she really wanted to laugh. Her impression of Arthur Taliesin was that he didn’t care at all what people thought of him, let alone whether people thought he was an asshole. Maggie did a very good job, though, of keeping her face neutral, reaching for her coffee to drink the last of it.


“I just wanted our students to see what was possible.”


Maggie froze, staring at Taliesin, her cup halfway to her mouth. How many times had she said the same thing about her Hawthorn students? There were some students who came to Hawthorn knowing exactly what they wanted, but most were a little aimless. They applied for college because it was the next Big Step, but they had no idea what they actually wanted to do. No idea what the possibilities even were. They were the kind of student she had been, before she knew what linguistics was. That Taliesin saw this, too, surprised Maggie.


“I absolutely should have prepared differently, but I don’t regret showing them big magic.” Then he added, “Or, trying to, anyway.” He sighed and rubbed his eyes beneath his glasses.


“Two of my former colleagues at Dartwood asked me to consult on research using one of the de novo energy conversion spells I’ve developed. They asked me to run the spells with a few elemental shifts, and I had reached a point in the work where I needed iron-derived gold.”


This was a spell he would have done a thousand times throughout the course of his research. It wasn’t even a de novo spell, but a legacy with a standardized incantation. The only reason it was considered class 3 spellwork was the energy required for the transformation. It should have been routine. It shouldn’t have been done in a classroom lab setting, but she could see his reasoning and understood why his students could benefit from seeing it. She could even see a way to do it safely, with a second professor and precautions in place. “Then what happened?”


Taliesin stared at a spot on the table. “My brother called during the incantation. I ignored the first call and kept reciting the spell, but I knew it was an emergency when the phone started ringing again. His mom, Lane, collapsed at work and was being rushed to the hospital. He was calling to ask me to meet him there.”


Maggie didn’t know what to do. His voice was so shaky, and he couldn’t keep his hands still. She found herself wanting to reach across the table and lace their fingers together, just to get him to stop moving, but she kept her hands around her coffee cup.


“I should have finished the damn incantation, or tied it off with magic, but I panicked. What if it had been Si—” He didn’t finish the thought, closing his eyes again.


“It doesn’t matter,” he finally continued. “I interrupted the incantation without properly tying off the spell and fumbled with my phone. I didn’t even get a chance to call Rory back before the spell fractured.” Taliesin sighed heavily, shaking his head as if he still couldn’t quite believe how it happened.


His voice was nearly trembling when he spoke again. “When my mom went into the hospital the first time, I was giving a lecture. I missed the first call from her. Then the second and the third. Everything that happened after was so quick…” He trailed off. “I know it’s a bad habit, but I started keeping my phone on during class. Just for phone calls from my dad and brother.”


He looked up for the first time since he began recounting that day. “Is your brother’s mom…” Maggie began.


“She’s okay. She received treatment for a minor medical condition, and other tests came back negative for anything more serious.” Maggie started to say something else, but Taliesin kept going. “Please don’t lecture me, Maggie. I know it was a series of bad decisions that I just made worse.”


Maggie bit her lip. She wished he didn’t think that the first words out of her mouth after he told her everything were going to be some kind of scolding. Even if he maybe deserved it. A little bit. “I wasn’t going to lecture you. I was just going to say that I’m glad Lane recovered.” He nodded, his look far off again. “Anyone might have made the same mistake.”


He let out a huff, something between a laugh and a groan. “Even you, Dr. Linden?”


She shivered, but even she couldn’t convince herself that it was the chill in the air with the fire roaring behind her. Why did it feel like she was missing something half the time he spoke? Why did she like the way he said her name so much?


She furrowed her brow. “You seem to think I make enough mistakes in the classroom.”


It was as much a reminder to herself as it was to him. This was the Arthur Taliesin who slashed the funding for her project. The same one who thought she was incapable of saying an incantation in an emergency. The one who judged her teaching.


He blinked, like he didn’t quite understand where the conversation had veered off track. Before he could argue, she went back to his documents and asked, “Can I see the original spell?”


Taliesin handed her another file folder. She ran her finger down the documents, looking briefly over the rune and alchemical equations that she only vaguely recognized until she got to the Diadhan incantation and its translation for the conversion spell. It was obvious from his story that the spell faltered with the incomplete incantation. “Where were you when the second call came in and you stopped the incantation?”


He reached across the table and pointed to a single line:



earthly shatter, fractured soil



She cringed. It was so much worse than she thought. Taliesin’s expression mirrored hers as she said, “Gods below, that’s the worst possible part of the incantation to mess up.”


“I know.”


“Stopping an incantation without tying off the spell, without giving that energy anywhere to go, could set off a pall at any point, but words have power. Shatter. Fractured. Gods below,” she repeated, “you’re lucky you didn’t open up a chasm to the underworld.” No wonder he thinks you’re a scold. He knew all of this, and it was clear he was already carrying so much guilt, but she couldn’t quite help the lecturing tone of her voice.


“In your professional opinion, do you think disrupting the incantation at that exact moment is the only reason the pall is so difficult to remove?”


She turned the problem over in her mind. “Alchemists and runologists often underestimate incantation errors. It’s the least precise part of spellmaking, but it’s that lack of precision that makes those errors just as dangerous as a miscalculation or an out-of-place mark.” She sighed, shaking her head. “I’m not surprised the pall is large. I’m not surprised it’s sticky. But a seven-foot fissure? Dissipation spells turning to dust? Without having looked at every single one of the details, I have to think there is something else feeding this pall and keeping it alive.”


“That’s what I think, too.”


“Do you have any theories?” she asked, almost excitedly, forgetting for a moment the seriousness of their task. Instead, it felt like collaborating with Dahlia on a project. Or when she consulted on incantations for de novo spells.


“What if it has something to do with Ilex Hall? Or Hawthorn?” he suggested. “My brother suggested the Wilds themselves could be influencing it.”


She tapped her finger idly as she considered this idea. “Have you visited the college historical center?” she asked as she shuffled through the file folders to look through anything from the Annex, a building that held a small museum and research center dedicated to Hawthorn, its founders, and Galloway. “We should check the records there.”


She looked up to see if he agreed and found him looking not at the scattered papers, but at her. Her cheeks flushed, again, at the intensity of his gaze. She sat back and crossed her arms, narrowing her eyes at him. Shut it down. “But don’t think I’ve forgotten about seeing the pall itself.”


It worked. The heady mix of something like tenderness and heat in his gaze vanished. “Let’s stick to the original plan. We’ll wait until campus empties after graduation. It’s safer that way.” Based on what he’d revealed about the pall this evening, she agreed that it made sense to wait to maintain the warding seal until the students were gone, but she didn’t understand why he seemed so anxious about her entering the pall. Was there something he didn’t want her to know about yet? Unless it was just some misplaced chivalry. The ghoul attack seemed to have shaken Taliesin more than her, and she was the one with a ghoul burn on her arm, not him. Well, he’d find out soon enough that she wasn’t some damsel who needed fussing over.


As if he could read where her thoughts wandered, Taliesin asked, “How is Rodrigo? Are his wards holding?”


That was the last thing she expected him to ask. “So far. He shut down for a day to clean up, but he opened back up in time for the next week. He said business is slow, though. People are feeling skittish.”


Taliesin looked around the quiet coffee shop. “This place should be full of students studying for finals. They should be loading up on caffeine and sugar.”


Finals week started Monday, and underclassman would move out the following weekend. The relief would be temporary, because families of graduating fourth-year students would begin to fill in the hotels and bed-and-breakfasts from Galloway to Atlantia in advance of the graduation ceremony. Campus would be quiet again in two weeks.


“The university historical center is closed during the summer,” she said. “If we want to start our investigation there, it has to be before they leave for the year.”


“Between visiting the historical center, finals, all that graduation prep we both have to do…” He trailed off, and there was a sly smirk on his face that made her want to throw a piece of paper at him. He let out a dramatic cough. “I can’t risk another bout of pall sickness so soon.”


She sighed theatrically, trying to tamp down her own grin. “Once again, Arthur Taliesin gets what he wants,” she said in a singsong, and his smirk widened into a smile. Her stomach fluttered, and something else in her stirred. How was he even more handsome when he smiled? She cleared her throat. “I’ll make us an appointment at the historical center.”


As Maggie began reorganizing the papers into manageable piles, trying very hard to not look at Taliesin, Liv walked over to their table with a bin to collect mugs and plates. “How was everything?”


“Perfect, as usual,” Taliesin said, and he seemed to have shed some of his earlier awkwardness. When Liv dropped a plate with a clatter, Taliesin interjected with an unfairly charming “Oh shoot!” and helped her stack the remaining dishes. Maggie smiled at the non-curse and suddenly found herself strangely grateful for an excuse to spend time with him. Even if she shouldn’t want that at all.


Liv turned to Maggie. “How do you know Little Artie?” Maggie couldn’t contain her smirk. There was nothing little about Arthur Taliesin.


Taliesin groaned, and Liv laughed. “Can we please leave Little Artie in the past? Maggie is my colleague at Hawthorn.”


“What is it you teach up there again?” Liv asked him.


“The required materials alchemy courses, mostly.”


Liv grimaced. “I nearly failed that class. Both semesters! But you were always smarter than us by half.” She said it warmly, but Maggie noticed Taliesin’s face fall slightly. Liv didn’t seem to see it, though, and went on. “I’m sure Simon loves having Uncle Artie in town all the time.”


“Not nearly as much as I love having him nearby.”


Liv continued chatting with Taliesin as they gathered their belongings. He reached out in an offer to carry Maggie’s bag, but she huffed and hiked it up her shoulder. At the door, Liv squeezed Taliesin’s arm and exchanged nice to meet yous and good nights with Maggie and Taliesin before locking the door behind them.
